4651: Paul mentions a letter "from Laodicea" in Colossians 4:16, but no such letter survives. Someone later filled the gap with a short letter of about 20 verses, stitched together from phrases in Philippians and Galatians. It appears in many medieval Latin Bibles and even early English ones, but the church never treated it as genuine Scripture.
4652:
The Latin Laodiceans is a patchwork (a "cento") of Paul's phrases: a greeting, thanks for the Laodiceans' faithfulness, a warning against vain talk, joy at Paul's imprisonment, an exhortation to do everything without grumbling, and a closing request that the letter be read to the Colossians. It contains nothing that is not in Paul's genuine letters and no doctrine of its own - which is the most obvious sign that it is an imitation.

It first appears in the Codex Fuldensis (AD 546) and then in many Latin Bible manuscripts from the sixth to the fifteenth centuries, sometimes between Colossians and 1 Thessalonians. It was included in the Wycliffite English Bibles and in some early printed German Bibles before the Reformation. The Muratorian fragment mentions a letter "to the Laodiceans" forged in Paul's name for Marcion's heresy, but that was probably a different work; Marcion himself called Ephesians "Laodiceans".

4658: Its weakness is obvious: it says nothing new and simply borrows Paul's words, so it adds no apostolic teaching. It has no early Greek manuscript tradition and was unknown to the Eastern churches. Jerome noted that some people read a letter to the Laodiceans but that everyone rejects it (*On Illustrious Men* 5). Even when copied into Latin Bibles, scholars such as Erasmus judged it inauthentic, and it disappeared from Bibles after the sixteenth century as both Protestant and Catholic editions standardised. The Council of Trent (1546) did not include it.
4659: It shows how the church's sense of the canon could be fuzzy at the edges in practice even while it was clear in principle: for nearly a thousand years many Western Christians would have seen it in their Bibles. It also illustrates the desire to recover the lost letter mentioned in Colossians. Some scholars think the real "letter from Laodicea" was Ephesians, a circular letter.

4684: 3 Corinthians is a short exchange of letters: the Corinthians tell Paul that teachers are denying the resurrection of the body, and "Paul" replies, defending Jesus' real birth from Mary and the bodily resurrection. It was written in the second century, probably as part of the Acts of Paul. The Armenian church long counted it in its New Testament, and the Syriac father Ephrem treated it as Paul's.
4685:
The Corinthians write that two men, Simon and Cleobius, are teaching that there is no resurrection of the flesh, that God did not create humans, that Jesus did not come in the flesh or was not born of Mary, and that the world is not God's. Paul, in prison at Philippi, answers that he handed on what he received: Jesus was born of Mary of the seed of David, the Holy Spirit came upon her, and he came to save all flesh. Using the image of a seed of wheat sown naked and rising clothed, and Jonah raised from the whale, he insists the body will rise.

The letters were evidently written to oppose Gnostic teaching on the body. They survive in Papyrus Bodmer X (third century), in the Coptic and Latin versions of the Acts of Paul, and in Armenian Bibles. Some scholars think they once circulated on their own; others think the author of the Acts of Paul wrote them.
4686: Letter of Stephanas and the elders: the teaching of Simon and Cleobius
4687: Paul in chains at Philippi receives the letter in distress
4688: Paul's reply: Jesus born of Mary by the Holy Spirit, from David's line
4689: Christ came to redeem all flesh; the prophets foretold him
4690: The resurrection: seed of wheat, Jonah, and the bones raised by Elisha's bones
4691: Warning: those who reject this teaching have no part in the resurrection
4692: It is pseudonymous: written in Paul's name a century after him, as part of the Acts of Paul, a work Tertullian exposed as the composition of an Asian presbyter. It was unknown to most Greek and Latin churches. However, its history is a real exception: Ephrem the Syrian in the fourth century commented on it as part of Paul's letters, and the Armenian church included it in its New Testament for centuries, often after 2 Corinthians. The modern Syriac churches do not include it, which is why it is marked rejected for them here, but this was not always the case.
4693: It is a vivid early defence of the goodness of creation, the incarnation and the resurrection of the body - core orthodox teaching. It shows how the Pauline letters were extended to fight later heresies, and it is an important example of how Eastern churches had slightly different canons in practice.

4722: The Abgar legend claims that King Abgar of Edessa, who was ill, wrote to Jesus asking him to come and heal him, and Jesus wrote back promising to send a disciple. After the resurrection, Addai (Thaddaeus) came, healed the king and converted the city. Eusebius found the letters in Edessa's archives and translated them around 300, but historians see them as a later legend explaining how Edessa became Christian.
4723:
In Eusebius' version, Abgar the Black, ruler of Edessa, hears of Jesus' healings and writes that Jesus must be God or the Son of God; he invites Jesus to live in his small, pleasant city, safe from the Jews who plot against him. Jesus replies that he is blessed for believing without seeing, that he must finish his mission, and that after his ascension he will send a disciple to heal him and bring life to his people. Thaddaeus (Addai in Syriac), one of the seventy, then comes and heals the king.

The later Syriac *Doctrine of Addai* (around 400) adds that Jesus' reply was delivered orally and that the messenger Hannan painted Jesus' portrait - the origin of the Image of Edessa, later called the Mandylion, a cloth with Jesus' face believed to be "not made by hands". Edessa did become an early Christian centre, but its first securely known Christians date from the late second century, and the real king Abgar who embraced Christianity may have been Abgar VIII (around 200), not the Abgar of Jesus' time.
4724: Abgar hears of Jesus and writes asking him to come and heal him

4729: No one in the early church treated it as Scripture, even though it claims to contain a letter written by Jesus himself. Augustine noted that no genuine writings of Jesus existed, and the Gelasian Decree lists the letter of Jesus to Abgar as apocryphal. Historians regard the correspondence as a legend from Edessa, written to give the city's church an apostolic founding. Syriac and other Eastern Christians have honoured the story as tradition rather than canon.
4730: It became Edessa's civic pride and protection: copies of Jesus' letter were inscribed on city gates and carried as charms, and it was even copied into amulets as far away as England. The Image of Edessa became one of the most important icons in Byzantium, and Orthodox churches keep a feast of the Holy Face on 16 August. It also preserves real memory of Edessa's importance in early Syriac Christianity.

4763: The Gospel of Thomas is a list of 114 sayings of Jesus with almost no stories, no crucifixion and no resurrection. About half resemble sayings in Matthew, Mark and Luke; others are strange and mystical, like "split a piece of wood, and I am there." A complete copy was found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945. Scholars disagree sharply about whether it preserves very early sayings or was written in the second century using the canonical Gospels.
4764:
It opens: these are the secret sayings that the living Jesus spoke and Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down; whoever finds their meaning will not taste death. The sayings call the reader to seek and find, to know oneself, to recognise that the kingdom is inside you and outside you and spread out on the earth unseen, and to return to the beginning, before the division of male and female. There are parables (the sower, the mustard seed, the wicked tenants), beatitudes, and puzzling sayings. Saying 13 has Jesus give Thomas three secret words; saying 114 ends with Peter saying women are not worthy of life and Jesus replying he will make Mary male - a line much debated today.

The complete Coptic text is the second tractate of Nag Hammadi Codex II, copied around 340-350; the Nag Hammadi library was found in a sealed jar in December 1945 by local farmers near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt - thirteen leather-bound codices holding over fifty texts. Greek fragments had already been found at Oxyrhynchus by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt in 1897-1904 (P.Oxy. 1, 654 and 655, from around 200-250), though they were only recognised as Thomas after 1945. Whether to call it "Gnostic" is itself debated: it lacks the full Gnostic creation myth, but its stress on saving knowledge and the soul's origin in the light fits later Gnostic readers who valued it.
4765: Prologue: the secret sayings of the living Jesus written by Thomas; saying 1: whoever finds their meaning will not taste death
4766: Seeking and finding; the kingdom within and outside (sayings 2-3)

4772: It was never in any canon list. Hippolytus (around 225) says a Gnostic group, the Naassenes, used a Gospel according to Thomas; Origen lists a Gospel of Thomas among heretical gospels; Eusebius puts it among works of heretics that are not even disputed but rejected (3.25.6); and Cyril of Jerusalem attributes it to the Manichaeans. Supporters of the canon's process stress that it lacks the story of Jesus' death and resurrection, central to the apostolic preaching, and that its spirituality of secret self-knowledge differs from the Gospels'. Scholars who favour an early date argue that its rejection reflects later theological conflict rather than its age, and that it could preserve some authentic sayings independently. Both groups agree that the Coptic text in its present form was shaped over time.
4773: It is the most important non-canonical Gospel for the study of Jesus' sayings. Some sayings may preserve independent or early forms of parables (for example, the parable of the wicked tenants without allegorical details). It has shaped modern spirituality and popular books, and debate over it raises the key questions of how early the canonical Gospels were recognised and what counts as "Christian" in the second century.

4803: The Gospel of Judas is a second-century Gnostic text in which Jesus laughs at the disciples' worship and reveals secret cosmic knowledge to Judas Iscariot. It was known only by name from Irenaeus until a Coptic copy, found in Egypt in the 1970s, was published in 2006. Scholars still argue whether it makes Judas a hero or a demon.
4804:
In the days before Passover Jesus finds the disciples giving thanks over bread and laughs, because they are worshipping the lesser god who made the world, not the true God. Only Judas recognises that Jesus comes from "the immortal realm of Barbelo". Jesus takes him aside and teaches him a Sethian creation story: an invisible great Spirit, a heavenly realm of aeons and luminaries, and lower rulers - including Nebro (or Yaldabaoth) and Saklas - who created the world and humanity. Jesus tells Judas he will "exceed" the others, for he will sacrifice the man that clothes Jesus. The text ends abruptly: Judas receives money and hands Jesus over.

The only surviving copy is in Codex Tchacos, which was reportedly found in the 1970s near El Minya in Middle Egypt, passed through dealers and a bank vault for decades and was badly damaged before being conserved and published by the National Geographic Society in 2006. The first translation presented Judas as Jesus' best friend and the true hero. Other Coptic scholars, notably April DeConick, argued that the translators had made errors: Judas is called "the thirteenth daimon" (demon), he is separated from the holy generation, and his act serves the hostile rulers. Many now read the text as a bitter satire on mainstream Christians.

It was never proposed as Scripture by any mainstream church.

It is important evidence for Sethian Gnostic thought and for second-century conflicts over the eucharist, sacrifice and church leadership. It also prompted a public conversation about Judas, betrayal and how scholars translate damaged manuscripts.

4839: The Gospel of Mary is a short second-century text, missing about half its pages, in which Mary Magdalene comforts the frightened disciples after Jesus leaves and shares a vision he gave her about the soul's ascent.
